instruction.text: How did Britain communicate in the Middle Ages? Select the man wearing green to find out.

atoms.b: This is a town crier. Their job was to read important announcements out ((++loud light)).
Most people in the Middle Ages could not read or ((++write listen)), so this was the only way for them to hear news.
People would then pass the message on to others in their ((++town tour)) , so the message eventually reached everyone.

instruction.text: Drag the letter to this messenger to find out more.

feedback.finish: Messengers were still being used in the Middle Ages to deliver letters. It was a difficult job, as they would often have to travel very far.

instruction.text: Communication took much longer in the Middle Ages. Read the reason why and select the matching image.

atoms.a: Letters, books and even laws would be handwritten and sent by messenger, which could take a very long time to reach people.
Books were copied out by people called scribes, who were mostly monks and nuns. Making just one book copy could take months!
There was no fixed way to spell words, which could make understanding messages difficult.

feedback.finish: Communication in the Middle Ages was difficult. Messages took ages to be delivered, very few people could even write, and spelling changed from person to person.

instruction.text: Drag the text to the printing press to print the words onto the paper.

atoms.b: The printing ((++press squash)) was brought to Britain in 1476. It worked by arranging letters into blocks, which would then be covered in ink and pressed onto paper to print sentences.
This meant that lots of books could be made quickly at the same ((++time rhyme)), so they became cheaper.
Many ((++more less)) people could then access information from books and learn to read and write.
It also helped people to agree on a fixed way of ((++spelling spoiling)) words, since everyone was reading the same printed spellings.
